title: Attention lets a token choose which context to read
summary: Understand why content-dependent access complements or replaces recurrent compression.

sections.title: Remembering everything in one state is difficult
paragraphs: A recurrent model carries the past through a fixed-width hidden state. Information needed much later must survive many updates, even when the model does not yet know it will matter. Attention provides a different access pattern: a representation can compare itself with stored representations and retrieve a weighted mixture. The computation can therefore focus on a relevant earlier phrase without requiring every detail to travel through one compact recurrent summary.

sections.title: Replace one fixed summary with a query-dependent one
paragraphs: Imagine translating a sentence containing two names. Different output words need different parts of the source. A query-dependent weighted sum can retrieve the relevant name at one step and a verb at another. In self-attention, every input position can construct such a summary from the same sequence. During teacher-forced training, many positions can be processed in parallel because their input tokens are already known; a causal mask still prevents access to future targets.

sections.title: Account for what attention costs
paragraphs: Dense attention compares many pairs of positions, creating quadratic pairwise work as sequence length grows. A recurrent state can be much more compact for streaming use. Attention also needs positional information or another mechanism to distinguish order; content comparisons alone do not encode a sequence's arrangement. Choose an architecture by the task's access pattern, memory budget, and latency requirements. The motivation for attention explains a useful trade-off rather than proving recurrent models are always inappropriate.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the alignment-and-translation paper for the problem it addresses, then compare the access pattern with the Transformer paper. The useful distinction is not simply old versus new architecture: it is whether a prediction must rely on one repeatedly compressed state or can retrieve from a collection of source representations. In the document-name example, identify where the name is stored and which computation makes it available to the answer.

Direct access still does not guarantee successful retrieval. The source representation must preserve the needed distinction, and the learned query-key comparison must give it useful weight. A system can have enough context capacity yet fail either requirement. When evaluating an attention-based design, vary the location of the relevant evidence and introduce plausible distractors. This separates the architectural possibility of accessing a token from the empirical claim that a trained model reliably uses that access.

exercise.prompt: A document question asks for a name mentioned near the beginning of a long passage. What advantage does attention offer, and what resource cost grows when every position can compare with every other?
exercise.answer: Attention can directly retrieve information associated with the earlier name instead of depending only on a repeatedly updated summary. Dense all-pairs comparisons grow quadratically with sequence length, and naive implementations also store quadratic attention matrices.

takeaways: Attention provides query-dependent access to context.
Its direct access pattern trades against pairwise computation and memory.

title: Queries ask, keys match, and values carry the information
summary: Separate the roles of Q, K, and V in a learned retrieval operation.

sections.title: Matching and content are different jobs
paragraphs: A query describes what a position wants to retrieve. A key describes how a source position should be matched. A value contains the information contributed if that source receives weight. All three are learned numerical representations, not literal database strings. Separating the matching space from the transmitted content lets a model decide relevance using one set of features while passing along another set.

sections.title: Project representations into three roles
paragraphs: For input \(X\) of shape \([B, T, D]\), learned matrices produce \(Q=XW_Q\), \(K=XW_K\), and \(V=XW_V\). Queries and keys must share their final width so their dot products are defined. Values may have a different final width. A query compares against all keys, softmax turns scores into weights, and those weights mix values. The output length follows the number of queries, not the number of stored keys.

sections.title: Do not confuse source identity with parameter sharing
paragraphs: In self-attention, \(Q\), \(K\), and \(V\) originate from the same sequence, but usually use different projections. Their rows therefore need not be identical. In cross-attention, queries may come from a text decoder while keys and values come from image features. Keys and values must remain aligned by source position; permuting one without the other changes which content a match retrieves. A large attention weight also does not establish a complete causal explanation of the model's answer.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the Transformer paper's attention definition to label the roles of each matrix before attaching a semantic story to a head. Queries determine the number of requested outputs; paired keys and values define the candidate memory. The six-query, ten-source example makes this clear because the score matrix cannot be square. A learned projection may change feature width, but it does not change which axis enumerates source positions.

A useful independent invariance check permutes keys and values together. The score columns and corresponding value rows change in matching order, leaving the final weighted mixture unchanged when masks and positional treatment are permuted consistently. Permuting keys alone usually changes the result because matching now retrieves the wrong content. This distinction is valuable when debugging a memory bank, image-patch sequence, or cached source representation: ordering is an association between keys and values, not an incidental tensor layout.

exercise.prompt: There are 6 queries, 10 keys, query/key width 8, and value width 12. What are the attention-score and output shapes without batch or head dimensions?
exercise.answer: The score matrix is \([6, 10]\), containing one score per query-key pair. Multiplying normalized scores by values \([10, 12]\) produces \([6, 12]\), one retrieved vector for each query.

takeaways: Queries and keys determine matching; values determine transmitted content.
Keys and values must preserve the same source ordering.

title: Compute scaled dot-product attention by hand
summary: Follow a complete numeric Q/K/V example from matching scores to a weighted output.

sections.title: One output is a weighted reading of the values
paragraphs: Attention first decides where to look, then combines what it finds. Queries and keys produce relevance scores; values supply the vectors being mixed. The weights for each query form a distribution over source positions. Before adding output projections, dropout, or other blocks, one attention row is therefore a convex combination of the value vectors. This simple property gives you a concrete way to check an implementation instead of memorizing its formula.

sections.title: Write the dimensions before the numbers
paragraphs: Ignore batches and heads for this example. Let \(Q\) and \(K\) each have shape \([2,2]\): there are two queries, two source positions, and query/key width \(d_k=2\). Let \(V\) also be \([2,2]\), so each source contributes a two-feature value. \(QK^{\top}\) has shape \([2,2]\), with rows indexing queries and columns indexing keys. Softmax acts across each row, and multiplying by \(V\) returns \([2,2]\).

sections.title: Turn two scores into one retrieved vector
paragraphs: Choose \(Q=K=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(V=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix}\). The first query has raw scores \([1, 0]\). Dividing by \(\sqrt2\) gives \([0.7071, 0]\). Exponentiation gives approximately \([2.0281, 1]\), and normalization produces approximately \([0.66976155, 0.33023845]\). Using unrounded weights, its output is approximately \([1.33952310, 1.32095380]\). The second query swaps the weights, producing approximately \([0.66047690, 2.67904620]\). Notice that the output mixes values, not keys.

sections.title: Why divide by the square root of the width?
paragraphs: Under a simple model with independent, zero-mean, unit-variance query and key coordinates, a dot product sums \(d_k\) terms and has variance \(d_k\). Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps that variance near one. Without the scaling, wider heads tend to generate more extreme logits, which can make softmax sharply concentrated and its gradients less useful. Real learned features need not satisfy those assumptions exactly; the argument motivates the scale rather than proving attention weights always remain well behaved.

sections.title: Mask and normalize the intended axis
paragraphs: Subtracting the largest logit before exponentiation improves numerical stability without changing softmax. Apply an additive mask before softmax so forbidden positions receive zero probability. In this example, a causal mask removes the first query's access to the second source: its weights become \([1, 0]\) and its output becomes \([2, 0]\). Check row sums and forbidden positions explicitly. An entirely masked row needs defined handling because naive softmax of all negative infinities is invalid.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Compare the scaled-attention equation in the Transformer paper with the official SDPA reference computation. Follow the normalization axis explicitly: each query needs a distribution over available keys. The numeric example here is small enough to inspect every intermediate, so it can serve as a reference when a batched or multi-head implementation is rearranged. Use unrounded intermediate values when comparing outputs; display rounding should happen only after the computation.

The library interface adds choices beyond the compact equation. A boolean participation mask differs from an additive bias, and dropout can change the row-sum and convex-mixture properties of the raw attention weights. SDPA applies the supplied dropout probability even if an enclosing module is in evaluation mode, so evaluation code must pass zero explicitly. An agreement test should therefore specify dtype, scale, mask, and dropout before interpreting a difference as evidence that the mathematical operation is wrong.

exercise.prompt: In the unmasked example, replace both value vectors by \([3,-1]\) while keeping \(Q\) and \(K\) unchanged. What does each output become, and why?
exercise.answer: Both outputs become \([3,-1]\). Each row's attention weights sum to one, so any weighted mixture of identical value vectors equals that same vector. Scores may differ, but there is no content difference for them to select.

takeaways: Scores come from \(Q\) and \(K\); output content comes from \(V\).
Softmax normalizes over source positions for each query.
Scaling controls the typical logit magnitude as head width changes.

title: Self-attention and cross-attention differ in where information comes from
summary: Trace the query stream separately from the key-value source in both attention patterns.

sections.title: Ask which representation is being updated
paragraphs: Self-attention updates a sequence using information from that same sequence. Cross-attention updates one sequence using a separate source. The mathematical weighted-sum operation can be identical; the distinction is the origin of its inputs. In a translation model, decoder states can ask questions of encoded source tokens. In a multimodal system, text queries can retrieve information from image patches.

sections.title: Output length follows the queries
paragraphs: Suppose a decoder has 5 token states and an image encoder produces 196 patch states. Cross-attention can project decoder states into \(Q [5, d_k]\), image states into \(K [196, d_k]\) and \(V [196, d_v]\), then produce 5 output vectors. Its score matrix is \([5, 196]\), not square. The two streams can have different original feature widths because their learned projection matrices map them into compatible matching dimensions.

sections.title: Apply masks according to the information policy
paragraphs: Decoder self-attention usually needs causality to avoid reading future target tokens. Cross-attention over a fully observed source generally does not need a triangular target-style mask, but it still needs to exclude padded source positions. A source containing future observations in a forecasting task may require additional restrictions. Shared source data can also allow precomputing cross-attention keys and values during generation; do not recompute them merely because a new query arrives.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the Transformer architecture description by tracing separate data streams through each attention use. In cross-attention, a decoder query retrieves from a source whose length and original width can differ from the target's. Mark those dimensions on the projection matrices as well as on \(Q\), \(K\), and \(V\). This prevents a common implementation shortcut from accidentally assuming identical source and target widths.

The masking policy follows what information is available, not the rectangular shape of the score matrix. A fully observed document can be visible to every summary position, while padded document slots remain invalid. For an online forecasting source, some observations might instead be unavailable at a particular prediction time. These are task-specific information constraints. Precomputing cross-attention keys and values is valid only while the encoded source and relevant model computation remain unchanged; a new source requires a new memory.

exercise.prompt: A text decoder has 8 queries and an audio encoder has 120 source frames. What score shape should cross-attention produce, and which length determines the number of output positions?
exercise.answer: The score matrix is \([8, 120]\), before batch and head axes. The output has 8 positions because each query receives one mixture of the 120 source values. The source length controls the number of retrieval candidates.

takeaways: Self versus cross describes input origin, not a different softmax rule.
Source padding and target causality are distinct masking requirements.

title: Multiple attention heads offer multiple matching spaces
summary: Understand head splitting, independent projections, and the trade-off between head count and head width.

sections.title: One mixture may combine incompatible relationships
paragraphs: A single attention distribution must allocate one set of weights across source positions. Multiple heads let the model construct several distributions in separate learned feature spaces, then combine their outputs. One head might become useful for local context while another captures a longer relationship, but such roles are learned possibilities rather than guaranteed human-readable assignments. The benefit comes from flexible parallel subspaces, not from naming heads after linguistic concepts.

sections.title: Split width, then recombine
paragraphs: With model width \(D = 96\) and \(H = 4\) heads, a common design uses head width 24. Projected \(Q\), \(K\), and \(V\) are rearranged from \([B, T, 96]\) to \([B, 4, T, 24]\). Each head computes its own \([T, T]\) attention matrix. Concatenating the four \([T, 24]\) outputs restores width 96, and an output projection mixes information across heads. Holding \(D\) fixed keeps many projection parameter counts unchanged when \(H\) changes.

sections.title: More heads are not free expressiveness
paragraphs: At fixed total width, adding heads makes each matching subspace narrower. It can also change kernel efficiency and attention-memory overhead. Some heads may become redundant, and good performance does not require every head to have a distinct interpretation. Check that \(D\) is divisible by \(H\) in a simple equal-width implementation, and transpose axes carefully when merging heads. Compare head counts under matched width and training budget to isolate the actual architectural change.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the multi-head construction in Attention Is All You Need to count matching spaces and projection dimensions separately. In the 96-wide example, four heads each receive 24 features, and the concatenated result returns to width 96. The output projection then combines those subspaces. This explains why increasing head count at fixed width does not automatically multiply the main projection-parameter budget.

Inspect intermediate storage as well as weights. An explicit implementation with more heads stores more separate attention maps, even though each map uses narrower query and value features. Head count can therefore alter memory and kernel behavior without changing the residual-stream width. A useful comparison holds width and training data fixed, records per-head width, and measures the actual implementation. Attractive visualizations of individual heads can suggest hypotheses, but they do not establish that every head has a stable, unique human-readable responsibility.

exercise.prompt: A model has width 128. Compare 4 heads and 8 heads under an equal-width split. What is the per-head width, and does the concatenated output width change?
exercise.answer: The head widths are 32 and 16 respectively. In both cases concatenation returns width 128. Increasing head count changes how the representation is partitioned, rather than automatically doubling the output width or the main projection matrices.

takeaways: Heads learn separate retrieval distributions.
At fixed model width, more heads mean narrower heads.

title: Masks define what a model is allowed to know
summary: Keep causal restrictions, padding restrictions, and library boolean conventions separate.

sections.title: A mask is an information boundary
paragraphs: A causal language model predicts a later token using only the available prefix. During training, all target tokens may already be present in memory, so the model needs an explicit restriction preventing future access. Padding creates another boundary: artificial positions should not contribute content merely because batching requires a rectangle. These masks solve different problems and often need to be combined.

sections.title: Mask scores before normalization
paragraphs: For an additive mask, allowed query-key pairs receive zero and forbidden pairs receive negative infinity before softmax. A square causal mask permits key index \(j\) only when \(j\le i\) for query index \(i\). A key-padding mask excludes padded source columns for every valid query. Padded query outputs may still exist, so exclude their targets from the loss separately. Cached decoding needs position-aware masks because query and key lengths may differ.

sections.title: Boolean values are API-specific
paragraphs: PyTorch's functional scaled_dot_product_attention uses True to mean a position participates, while MultiheadAttention key_padding_mask uses True to mean ignore that position. Reusing one boolean mask unchanged can reverse the information policy. Test with a tiny sequence whose future token is deliberately altered: earlier causal outputs should remain unchanged. Also handle rows with no valid keys explicitly, because a naive softmax over entirely masked entries can produce undefined values.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the two PyTorch attention interfaces side by side before reusing a boolean tensor. In SDPA, True permits participation; in MultiheadAttention's key-padding mask, True excludes a position. A mask with the right shape can therefore implement precisely the opposite information policy after an API change. Verify a small example with clearly distinguishable values instead of inferring the convention from the argument name.

The non-square causal case deserves a separate test. SDPA's upper-left causal alignment for one query and several keys allows only the first key; it does not automatically interpret that query as the newest cached position. For incremental decoding, construct the intended position-aware permission rule or use an appropriate cache-aware interface. A query at the current final position may read the entire valid prefix. Keep that causal decision separate from excluding padded keys and ignoring padded targets in the loss.

exercise.prompt: For a four-token causal sequence with zero-based indices, which key positions may query index 2 read? If index 1 is padding, which of those remain valid?
exercise.answer: Causality permits keys 0, 1, and 2. Excluding the padded key leaves 0 and 2. Key 3 remains forbidden by causality even though it is not padding.

takeaways: Causal masks and padding masks enforce different boundaries.
Verify boolean conventions and test causality with changed future tokens.

title: Encoder and decoder blocks are information-flow patterns
summary: Read architecture names through their attention masks and the sources they can access.

sections.title: The task determines what is visible
paragraphs: An encoder usually builds representations of an observed input with bidirectional self-attention. A decoder used for autoregressive generation restricts self-attention to the available prefix. An encoder-decoder model separates an observed source from a generated target and adds cross-attention connecting them. These labels describe common patterns, so inspect the actual block and objective rather than assuming the name alone specifies every implementation detail.

sections.title: Trace a translation computation
paragraphs: An encoder converts a source sentence of length \(S\) into \(S\) contextual vectors. The decoder processes target-prefix states of length \(T\) with causal self-attention, then uses cross-attention over the encoded source. The target stream therefore has both a \([T, T]\) masked interaction and a \([T, S]\) source interaction. During teacher-forced training, all target positions are computed together; during generation, the target grows one token at a time.

sections.title: A decoder-only model still conditions on input
paragraphs: A prompt and its continuation can share one causal sequence, so decoder-only does not mean input-free. Conversely, an encoder's bidirectional representations cannot simply be used for next-token prediction without controlling target leakage. Architecture also affects reusable computation: an encoder-decoder can encode a fixed source once, while the decoder repeatedly retrieves from it. Compare systems with the same task framing, because different source-target formatting can change both cost and available information.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the encoder and decoder portions of the Transformer paper as a diagram of permitted information flow. A source token can be contextualized using the fully observed source, while a target prediction must respect the generated prefix. The extra cross-attention path lets a target state retrieve source information without treating the entire source as previously generated target tokens. Trace those permissions before comparing parameter counts.

The training objective must agree with the mask and target alignment. A lower-triangular self-attention mask allows a position to see its own input token, so next-token labels must be shifted appropriately to avoid asking the model to copy an already visible target. Teacher forcing permits parallel training because the inputs are known, not because future targets become legitimate conditioning information. When reading a decoder-only adaptation, inspect how prompt tokens, continuation tokens, and loss-masked positions are arranged within that same causal sequence.

exercise.prompt: For summarization, identify the source and target streams in an encoder-decoder model. Which stream can use bidirectional attention, and which must preserve causal generation?
exercise.answer: The document is the observed source and can be encoded bidirectionally. The summary is the generated target and uses causal self-attention over its prefix, plus cross-attention to the document representation.

takeaways: Architecture names summarize access patterns.
A causal prompt can provide conditioning without a separate encoder.

title: Position encodings give order to content-based attention
summary: Compare learned position vectors with sinusoidal coordinates and their extrapolation limits.

sections.title: Content alone does not specify order
paragraphs: If a self-attention layer has no positional signal and no order-dependent mask, consistently permuting its input positions permutes its outputs rather than teaching it that one token came first. Many tasks need ordering: exchanging subject and object can change a sentence's meaning. Position encodings provide a coordinate system alongside token content so the model can distinguish identical tokens appearing at different locations.

sections.title: Add a coordinate vector to each token
paragraphs: A learned absolute-position table stores one vector per supported position and adds it to the token embedding. Sinusoidal encoding instead fills paired coordinates with sine and cosine functions at different frequencies. The multiple frequencies provide both fast-changing local signals and slower-changing long-range signals. Addition preserves model width, but mixes position and content in the representation consumed by later projections.

sections.title: Representing a position is not mastering it
paragraphs: A sinusoidal formula can be evaluated beyond the training length, but that does not guarantee accurate long-context behavior. Learned tables have an explicit range unless extended or interpolated. Position indices also need to remain consistent when padding, packing, or caching sequences. Test a model with the same content placed at different positions and lengths; a failure can reflect training distribution, positional treatment, or attention access rather than an insufficient vocabulary.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Inspect the positional-encoding formula in the Transformer paper together with the surrounding attention computation. The sine and cosine coordinates are added to token representations before learned projections, so their effects need not remain cleanly separated from content. At position zero, each sine coordinate is zero and each corresponding cosine coordinate is one; later positions change the combination at multiple frequencies.

An informative comparison separates representing an index from using it successfully. A sinusoidal formula produces coordinates for position 600 without a table lookup, but that only removes an indexing limitation. It does not establish that the trained model can retrieve evidence at unfamiliar distances. Likewise, extending a learned table changes what inputs can be represented without automatically supplying training experience for them. Evaluate content placed at several offsets and lengths while keeping the task itself fixed; this makes positional behavior more interpretable than a single maximum-context number.

exercise.prompt: A learned position table has shape \([512, 64]\). What fails when an unmodified model indexes position 600? Why does a sinusoidal formula avoid that specific failure without guaranteeing good predictions?
exercise.answer: The table has no row 600, so direct lookup is out of range. A sinusoidal formula can compute that position without a stored row, but the model may still behave poorly because it never learned to use such positions or distances.

takeaways: Position encoding makes order available to the model.
A computable position is not necessarily a well-trained position.

title: RoPE makes query-key interactions depend on relative position
summary: Understand rotary position embeddings through paired-coordinate rotations and their effect on dot products.

sections.title: Rotate the matching coordinates
paragraphs: Rotary position embedding applies a position-dependent rotation to pairs of query and key coordinates. A rotation changes direction while preserving length. When a query and key at different positions are compared, their relative rotation influences the dot product. Position therefore enters the matching operation directly, rather than only through an absolute vector added to the residual stream.

sections.title: Relative angles survive the dot product
paragraphs: For a two-dimensional pair, rotate \(x\) by angle \(\theta\) using \([x_1\cos\theta-x_2\sin\theta,\ x_1\sin\theta+x_2\cos\theta]\). If query position \(m\) uses rotation \(R_m\) and key position \(n\) uses \(R_n\), their dot product becomes \(q^{\top}R_m^{\top}R_nk=q^{\top}R_{n-m}k\) when the angles are linear in position. Different coordinate pairs use different frequencies, providing multiple distance scales. Values are typically left unrotated in the common formulation.

sections.title: Cached positions must remain consistent
paragraphs: During incremental decoding, a newly computed query must use its actual position, not restart from zero. Cached keys need the corresponding rotations from their own positions. Mixing a rotated cache with an inconsistent indexing convention corrupts matching even when tensor shapes look correct. RoPE also does not eliminate long-context limits: changing the frequency schedule or extending context requires careful evaluation of retrieval and task accuracy across positions.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read RoFormer by following the two-dimensional rotation before expanding to many coordinate pairs. The relative-angle identity in this article can be checked using ordinary rotation matrices: a shared rotation cancels from the dot product, while different rotations leave their angle difference. That is the mechanism to identify when examining a library's paired-coordinate layout or a checkpoint's rotary convention.

The relative-position statement concerns the interaction of given query and key vectors. Those vectors can themselves already contain contextual information, so it does not imply that every attention score is solely a function of distance. For a cache test, compare one full-sequence evaluation with token-by-token evaluation using the same absolute indices and frequencies. Restarting the query position at zero changes the rotation even if all shapes remain valid. Context extensions that change frequencies should be evaluated as changed model behavior, not assumed to preserve the original retrieval geometry.

exercise.prompt: Let \(q = k = [1, 0]\). Rotate \(q\) by 0 degrees and \(k\) by 90 degrees. What is their dot product? What happens if both are rotated by 90 degrees?
exercise.answer: With different rotations, the vectors are \([1, 0]\) and \([0, 1]\), so the dot product is zero. If both rotate by 90 degrees, both become \([0, 1]\) and the dot product is one. The shared rotation cancels; the relative angle matters.

takeaways: RoPE rotates query and key coordinate pairs.
Correct cache position offsets are essential during decoding.

title: Normalization placement changes the residual path
summary: Compare pre-norm and post-norm blocks by writing the exact order of their operations.

sections.title: The same ingredients can make a different network
paragraphs: A Transformer block combines a residual connection, normalization, and a learned sublayer such as attention. Moving normalization changes the function and its gradient paths even if parameter counts remain similar. Pre-norm normalizes the branch input before the sublayer, while post-norm normalizes after the branch output is added to the residual. This is an architectural choice, not merely a cosmetic code rearrangement.

sections.title: Follow the identity route
paragraphs: In pre-norm, \(y=x+F(\operatorname{LN}(x))\), so \(x\) has a direct additive path to \(y\). In post-norm, \(y=\operatorname{LN}(x+F(x))\), so the entire result passes through normalization. Their Jacobians therefore differ: the normalization derivative lies outside the addition in post-norm. Pre-norm stacks commonly use a final normalization after the blocks. The overall behavior also depends on initialization, residual scaling, depth, and optimizer schedule.

sections.title: Do not swap the order inside a checkpoint
paragraphs: Weights trained under one placement generally cannot be moved into the other computation while preserving predictions. When reproducing a paper or loading weights, inspect the exact equations and final normalization. For a controlled comparison, initialize both systems consistently and track gradient norms by depth during the first updates. Pre-norm often improves optimization behavior in deep setups, but it does not imply that every pre-norm model can safely discard warmup or use an arbitrary learning rate.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the pre-LN/post-LN paper with the residual sum highlighted. Moving normalization from after the sum to inside the branch changes which operations lie on the direct path. The zero-branch example here makes that distinction observable without training: \(x + 0\) preserves the representation, whereas \(\operatorname{LN}(x+0)\) generally does not. This is a property of the written computation, not a claim about a particular optimizer.

The paper's optimization observations should be interpreted together with the tested architecture and initialization. A result showing that one setup trains without warmup does not imply that any pre-norm checkpoint can tolerate arbitrary learning rates or residual scales. When comparing implementations, inspect both sublayers and the final normalization outside the block stack. A seemingly minor mismatch there can change predictions even when every tensor loads successfully and all parameter names and shapes appear compatible.

exercise.prompt: If the residual branch \(F\) returns zero, what does each block output? What does this reveal about the identity path?
exercise.answer: Pre-norm returns \(x\) exactly. Post-norm returns \(\operatorname{LN}(x)\), which generally differs from \(x\). The zero-branch case exposes the direct identity path present in pre-norm and the normalization applied to that path in post-norm.

takeaways: Operation order determines gradient flow.
Normalization placement must match the architecture used to train a checkpoint.

title: The Transformer FFN transforms features at each position
summary: Understand why token mixing and positionwise nonlinear computation are complementary.

sections.title: Retrieval is followed by local processing
paragraphs: Attention mixes information across token positions. A feed-forward network then transforms the resulting feature vector independently at each position using shared weights. The FFN does not create a new direct path between tokens, but its input already contains context gathered by attention. Alternating these operations lets the model retrieve relevant information and then compute richer features from that contextual representation.

sections.title: Expand, activate, and project back
paragraphs: A common FFN maps model width \(D\) to hidden width \(F\), applies a nonlinear activation, then maps back to \(D\). With input \([B, T, D]\), the intermediate is \([B, T, F]\) and the output returns to \([B, T, D]\), enabling a residual addition. Ignoring biases, the two matrices contain \(2DF\) parameters. For \(D = 256\) and \(F = 1024\), that is 524,288 weights in one FFN.

sections.title: Positionwise does not mean context-free
paragraphs: The same FFN parameters are reused at every position, but different contextual inputs yield different activations. Increasing \(F\) adds representational capacity and substantial matrix-multiplication cost; attention is not automatically the dominant cost at short sequence lengths. When profiling, measure projections and FFNs separately from pairwise attention. Avoid accidentally flattening the token and feature axes into one dimension, which changes a shared positionwise network into a sequence-length-specific operation.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the positionwise feed-forward description in the Transformer paper while keeping the token axis visible. The same two matrices are applied at every position; the hidden width expands features, not sequence length. The parameter count \(2DF\) therefore does not include a factor of \(T\), although the amount of computation does. This is a useful distinction when estimating the cost of processing a longer prompt.

A contextual input can make an FFN's output depend indirectly on distant tokens even though the FFN itself never mixes positions. To isolate that fact, compare the same token representation before and after an attention layer has incorporated another token's information. The subsequent positionwise operation receives different inputs and can produce different features. When profiling a Transformer, keep the FFN and projection costs separate from pairwise attention; a long-context complexity argument does not establish which component dominates a short-sequence workload.

exercise.prompt: An FFN maps width 64 to 256 and back to 64 with biases on both layers. How many parameters does it contain, and which dimensions change for input \([2, 10, 64]\)?
exercise.answer: The count is \(64\cdot256+256+256\cdot64+64=33{,}088\). The hidden tensor is \([2, 10, 256]\), then the output is \([2, 10, 64]\). Batch size and sequence length do not change.

takeaways: Attention mixes positions; FFNs transform per-position features.
FFN width affects both parameter count and compute.

references.title: Attention Is All You Need
references.note: Read the positionwise feed-forward sublayer and its expansion/projection structure.

title: SwiGLU adds an input-dependent gate to the FFN
summary: Trace the two expansion branches and the elementwise interaction in a gated MLP.

sections.title: Let one feature stream modulate another
paragraphs: A conventional FFN applies one activation to one expansion. A gated FFN creates two learned feature streams and multiplies them elementwise before projecting back. One stream supplies content while the other controls its strength. Because both depend on the input, the interaction can express patterns that a single activated projection handles differently. The gate is a learned continuous computation, not a manually specified feature selector.

sections.title: Count three matrices instead of two
paragraphs: A common SwiGLU expression is \([\operatorname{SiLU}(xW_g)\odot xW_u]W_d\), ignoring biases. Both expansion branches have width \(F\), and the down projection returns to model width \(D\). This uses roughly \(3DF\) weights, compared with \(2DF\) for a standard two-matrix FFN at the same \(F\). To match parameter budgets, the gated hidden width must therefore be smaller than the ungated width. A fair comparison should state which quantity is held constant.

sections.title: A gate need not lie between zero and one
paragraphs: \(\operatorname{SiLU}(x)=x\sigma(x)\) can be negative and can exceed one, so a SwiGLU gate is not simply a Bernoulli-style probability. Its multiplicative interaction changes activation and gradient scales. Check initialization, normalization, and kernel support when replacing an FFN. Also verify which projection is gated: interchanging weights in a trained checkpoint changes the function, even though the multiplication itself is commutative after both branches have been computed.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read GLU Variants Improve Transformer by identifying the two expanded feature streams and the final down projection. The SwiGLU expression in this article uses SiLU on one branch before elementwise multiplication. Swapping the raw projection weights changes which stream passes through the nonlinearity, so commutativity of multiplication does not justify exchanging those weights in a trained model.

The three-matrix parameter count provides a concrete way to interpret a reported comparison. At the same hidden width, a gated FFN has more weights than a conventional two-matrix FFN; reducing the width can match that budget. The 1536-to-1024 example follows from equating those counts, before biases and hardware rounding. It does not prove equal latency or identical representational capacity. Inspect the actual hidden widths, activation choice, and measured runtime before attributing an improvement exclusively to gating rather than to a changed parameter or compute budget.

exercise.prompt: An ordinary FFN uses hidden width 1,536. Ignoring biases, what SwiGLU hidden width gives the same parameter count at a fixed model width \(D\)?
exercise.answer: Equate \(2D\cdot1536\) with \(3D\cdot F\), giving \(F = 1024\). Both then use \(3{,}072D\) weights. Real architectures may round widths for hardware efficiency, so verify the actual configuration rather than assuming an exact ratio.

takeaways: SwiGLU multiplies two input-dependent feature streams.
Match parameter or compute budgets when comparing FFN variants.

references.title: GLU Variants Improve Transformer

title: MHA, MQA, and GQA trade key-value diversity for cache efficiency
summary: Keep query-head count separate from the number of key and value heads.

sections.title: Queries can share the same memory representation
paragraphs: Multi-head attention usually gives each query head its own keys and values. During decoding, storing and repeatedly reading all those key-value heads can be expensive. Multi-query attention shares one key head and one value head across all query heads. Grouped-query attention uses an intermediate number of key-value heads, with each pair shared by a group of query heads.

sections.title: Separate two head counts in the shapes
paragraphs: Let \(H_q=16\) and \(H_{\text{kv}}=4\). Queries have shape \([B,16,T_q,d]\), while keys and values use \([B,4,T_k,d]\). Each group of four query heads attends to the same key-value head while retaining its own query projection. MHA corresponds to \(H_{\text{kv}}=H_q\); MQA corresponds to \(H_{\text{kv}}=1\). At fixed lengths, layers, and dtype, cache size scales with \(H_{\text{kv}}\).
sections.formula: \text{KV cache elements}=2\cdot\text{layers}\cdot B\cdot T\cdot H_{\text{kv}}\cdot d

sections.title: Cache savings do not guarantee proportional speedups
paragraphs: Reducing key-value heads shrinks cache storage and associated bandwidth, but query projections, output projections, FFNs, and other work remain. Quality can also change because heads share part of the representation. A naive implementation that physically repeats keys and values may lose the intended memory benefit. Check whether the attention kernel supports grouped heads, and compare end-to-end decoding at matched batch size, context length, and precision.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Compare the multi-query decoding paper with GQA by counting query heads and key-value heads independently. The cache equation uses \(H_{\text{kv}}\) because future queries reuse stored keys and values, not old queries. In the sixteen-query-head, four-KV-head example, each group shares a source representation while retaining distinct query projections. This is a structural sharing choice rather than a reduction in the number of generated output positions.

The ideal cache ratio is only one component of an efficiency claim. Physically repeating KV tensors to imitate grouped heads can increase temporary memory or traffic, while specialized kernels may preserve the sharing more effectively. Query projections, output projections, and FFNs also remain. Read quality and runtime results as measurements under specified architecture and serving conditions. A fourfold reduction in cache elements does not establish a fourfold reduction in request latency, especially when weights or other operations dominate the workload.

exercise.prompt: A model switches from 32 key-value heads to 8 while keeping all other cache dimensions fixed. What is the ideal cache-size ratio? Does total model inference time necessarily improve by the same factor?
exercise.answer: The cache becomes \(\frac8{32}=\frac14\), or one quarter of its previous size. Total inference time need not fall fourfold because other computation, memory transfers, and kernel overhead remain, and the original workload may not have been cache-bandwidth limited.

takeaways: Query-head count and key-value-head count are distinct.
GQA provides a continuum between MHA and MQA.

title: A KV cache reuses the past without recomputing it
summary: Identify the saved computation, growing memory, and conditions that make cached decoding valid.

sections.title: Old causal states do not need future tokens
paragraphs: In a causal decoder, a past token's hidden representation depends only on its prefix. Appending a new token does not change that old computation in deterministic evaluation. Each layer can therefore keep previously computed keys and values. The new token supplies a new query and new key-value pair, then reads the stored history. This avoids repeatedly processing the complete prefix through every layer.

sections.title: Append memory at each layer
paragraphs: For one new token, \(Q\) has query length one, while the key-value sequence length is the existing context plus that token. Attention still compares the new query with all allowed cached keys and mixes the corresponding values. The cache stores keys and values rather than past queries because future steps need the former as retrieval memory. Cache storage grows linearly with sequence length, layer count, batch size, key-value heads, and head width.
sections.formula: \text{Cache bytes}=2\cdot L\cdot B\cdot T\cdot H_{\text{kv}}\cdot d_{\text{head}}\cdot\text{bytes per element}

sections.title: Consistency matters more than the container type
paragraphs: Position indices, masks, model weights, and preprocessing must match between full and cached evaluation. Changing an earlier token invalidates affected cached states. Training-time dropout or changing parameters also breaks straightforward reuse assumptions. Compare last-token logits from a full-prefix forward pass with incremental cached logits on a tiny example. Small numerical differences can arise from kernels, but a large mismatch usually indicates an indexing or masking error.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the incremental-decoding discussion in the multi-query paper to identify exactly what is reused. Each layer keeps historical keys and values because a new query needs to compare with that history and retrieve its content. Past queries are not the memory needed for later attention. The byte-count example here makes the two stored tensors explicit and keeps sequence length, layer count, KV-head count, and element size as separate factors.

A cache-validity test should compare the same prediction, not merely two sequences of plausible generated tokens. Feed an identical prefix to a full forward pass and an incremental computation, then compare the next-token logits under matching positions and masks. If an earlier token or model parameter changes, dependent cached states are stale. Deterministic evaluation removes dropout randomness but does not remove floating-point differences caused by different kernel shapes. Small tolerances can be appropriate; a large mismatch needs a causal explanation.

exercise.prompt: A 2-layer model with batch 1, sequence length 100, 4 KV heads, head width 8, and 2-byte elements stores how many cache bytes? Ignore allocator overhead.
exercise.answer: The cache stores \(2\cdot2\cdot1\cdot100\cdot4\cdot8=12{,}800\) elements, counting keys and values. At 2 bytes each, that is 25,600 bytes. Doubling context length doubles this storage.

takeaways: Caching saves repeated prefix computation.
It adds memory that grows with context and must remain position-consistent.

title: Prefill and decode stress different parts of a serving system
summary: Separate prompt processing from incremental token generation when measuring latency.

sections.title: One request contains two workloads
paragraphs: Prefill processes the known prompt, builds contextual states, and initializes the KV cache. Decode repeatedly generates additional tokens using that cache. The prompt's tokens are available together, while each generated token depends on earlier generated choices. This difference changes parallelism and latency. A single average tokens-per-second number can hide whether a system is slow to begin responding or slow between subsequent tokens.

sections.title: Compare the matrix shapes
paragraphs: During prefill, many queries attend over the prompt, allowing relatively large matrix operations. During a single-sequence decode step, query length is often one, so the model repeatedly reads weights and an expanding cache to produce one next-token distribution. Larger decode batches can improve utilization but consume more cache memory and may affect latency. Workload regimes therefore depend on batch, prompt length, output length, architecture, and hardware rather than on a universal compute-versus-memory label.

sections.title: Report user-visible timing separately
paragraphs: Measure time to first token, time between generated tokens, complete request latency, and throughput under a stated concurrency level. Include tokenization, queuing, and transfer overhead when they matter to the user experience. Warm up kernels and synchronize timing boundaries appropriately. A short-prompt benchmark with long outputs emphasizes decode; a long-document summarization request can be dominated by prefill. Benchmark both if the application serves both.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference alongside the multi-query decoding cost analysis, keeping the number of simultaneous queries in mind. A prompt offers many known positions to process together, while one sequence's next generated token depends on the previous choice. The distinction changes matrix shapes and opportunities to reuse loaded data. FlashAttention provides a complementary perspective on attention's memory traffic, but an attention-kernel improvement alone is not a complete serving-system latency result.

For the timing example, explicitly define whether the first emitted token is included in startup time. With that convention, an \(N\)-token answer takes approximately \(0.2+\frac{N-1}{20}\) seconds on A and \(1+\frac{N-1}{50}\) seconds on B. Their crossover is between 27 and 28 tokens. This calculation illustrates why both time to first token and subsequent token rate matter. Real comparisons must also state concurrency, queueing, prompt lengths, output lengths, and any batching policy.

exercise.prompt: System A reaches the first token in 0.2 seconds and then emits 20 tokens per second. System B takes 1 second initially and emits 50 tokens per second. Which is faster for a very short answer versus a long answer?
exercise.answer: A tends to finish a very short answer sooner because its startup cost is lower. B can finish a sufficiently long answer sooner because its per-token generation cost is lower. The crossover depends on the exact number of generated tokens and timing convention.

takeaways: Prefill and decode have different parallelism and memory behavior.
Report startup latency and incremental generation speed separately.

title: FlashAttention saves memory traffic without approximating attention
summary: Distinguish the mathematical operation from the way a GPU executes and stores its intermediates.

sections.title: Moving numbers can cost more than multiplying them
paragraphs: A naive attention implementation writes a large score matrix to GPU memory, applies softmax, and reads another large matrix to mix values. Those intermediates can be expensive even when the GPU has ample arithmetic capacity. FlashAttention reorganizes the same attention computation into tiles that fit faster on-chip memory, reducing transfers to and from high-bandwidth memory. Its goal is an execution improvement, not a sparse approximation to which tokens interact.

sections.title: Normalize incrementally across tiles
paragraphs: A row's softmax normally needs a maximum and a sum across all keys. Online softmax can maintain those statistics while visiting key blocks. When a new block changes the running maximum, previously accumulated sums and weighted values are rescaled consistently. This permits exact attention in real arithmetic without materializing the full attention matrix. The backward pass can recompute selected intermediates rather than storing everything from the forward pass.

sections.title: Quadratic arithmetic still exists
paragraphs: Dense FlashAttention still performs all relevant query-key interactions, so its pairwise arithmetic remains quadratic in sequence length. It reduces memory use and I/O, not the fundamental number of dense pairs. Floating-point operation order can produce small numerical differences from a reference implementation. Speed also depends on dimensions, dtype, masks, and supported hardware. Compare outputs and gradients on a small case, then measure peak memory and end-to-end runtime on the target workload.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the FlashAttention algorithm by tracking what crosses the boundary between fast on-chip storage and main GPU memory. The compact attention equation does not require a particular schedule of intermediate writes. Tiling changes that schedule, while online normalization preserves the required weighted sum. When a new tile raises a row's running maximum from \(m\) to \(m'\), old exponential accumulations must be rescaled consistently by \(\exp(m-m')\).

That accounting is the key distinction from approximations that remove token interactions. A dense tiled implementation still considers the relevant query-key pairs, so doubling sequence length does not remove the quadratic arithmetic growth. Numerical equality should also be interpreted carefully: changed operation ordering can affect floating-point results even when the real-arithmetic expression is the same. Use a small output-and-gradient comparison to investigate semantics, then measure memory and runtime on the actual supported hardware. The first check cannot establish a GPU speedup.

exercise.prompt: If sequence length doubles, does using FlashAttention make the dense pairwise computation grow only linearly? Explain which resource improvement the algorithm primarily targets.
exercise.answer: No. The number of query-key pairs still grows by about four times. FlashAttention avoids storing full quadratic intermediates and reduces memory traffic through tiling and recomputation, while preserving dense attention semantics.

takeaways: Exact attention can have different execution schedules.
Lower memory traffic does not imply linear attention arithmetic.

title: Attention complexity depends on which operation you count
summary: Separate projections, pairwise attention, activations, and incremental cache costs.

sections.title: One big-O label is not a memory budget
paragraphs: A Transformer layer includes feature projections, pairwise token interactions, an FFN, and storage for backward or decoding. Saying attention is quadratic identifies one important growth pattern but does not describe the entire layer. At short sequences, width-dependent projections and FFNs can dominate. At long sequences, all-pairs attention and its intermediates become increasingly important. State which dimensions vary before comparing complexity claims.

sections.title: Write the dominant terms
paragraphs: For sequence length \(T\) and model width \(D\), standard projections cost roughly \(\mathcal{O}(TD^2)\). With total head width \(D\), score computation and value mixing cost \(\mathcal{O}(T^2D)\). Naively storing attention weights requires \(\mathcal{O}(BHT^2)\) elements, while a KV cache is linear in \(T\). For \(B = 2\), \(H = 8\), \(T = 1024\), the full FP16 attention-weight tensor for one layer contains 16 matrices of size \(1024\times1024\) and occupies 32 MiB. Each individual matrix occupies 2 MiB; these counts exclude logits, gradients, and every other layer.

sections.title: Training and decoding need different accounting
paragraphs: Training often retains activations for backpropagation. A cached decode step uses one new query, so its attention work grows roughly linearly with the current context length, but generating many tokens sums that cost over growing prefixes. Efficient kernels can avoid storing quadratic matrices without removing pairwise arithmetic. Report actual peak memory and latency together with theoretical counts; memory allocation, fusion, bandwidth, and batch scheduling all affect observed results.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the Transformer complexity comparison and the FlashAttention memory discussion as statements about different resources. The pairwise \(\mathcal{O}(T^2D)\) term counts interactions, whereas \(\mathcal{O}(BHT^2)\) describes one explicitly stored attention tensor. Eliminating that tensor from memory does not eliminate the interactions. Conversely, a KV cache has a different purpose and grows linearly with retained context for a fixed architecture.

Use the 32 MiB example as an accounting exercise rather than a prediction of total device memory. It includes the full batched, multi-head FP16 attention-weight tensor for one layer and excludes other layers, logits, saved activations, gradients, optimizer state, and allocator overhead. A training-memory estimate and a decoding-memory estimate should list different categories. For generation, also distinguish cost per step from cost over the whole continuation: one new query scans a growing context, and summing many such steps accumulates the work. Theoretical scaling becomes useful only after those boundaries are stated.

exercise.prompt: With width and batch fixed, sequence length rises from 512 to 2048. How do dense pairwise work, projection work, and KV-cache storage scale approximately?
exercise.answer: Length increases fourfold. Dense pairwise work grows sixteenfold, projection work grows fourfold, and KV-cache storage grows fourfold. These ratios describe the stated components, not necessarily total wall-clock time.

takeaways: Separate width-dependent and length-dependent costs.
Training activation memory and inference cache memory are different budgets.

title: Build a Transformer block whose invariants you can test
summary: Assemble attention, normalization, residuals, and an FFN while checking shapes and causality.

sections.title: Build a block before building a language model
paragraphs: A Transformer block accepts contextual vectors and returns vectors of the same width. It does not by itself provide tokenization, embeddings, positional information, or a vocabulary loss. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the first implementation easier to inspect. Start with one head and no dropout, then verify the computation before adding multiple heads, caching, or optimized kernels.

sections.title: Use a small pre-norm construction
paragraphs: The example below normalizes before each sublayer, computes Q/K/V with one projection, applies a causal attention mask, and adds two residual updates. All tensors preserve batch and sequence axes, and the FFN expands only features. The code intentionally uses explicit attention matrices to expose the mechanism. For a complete language model, add positional information to the incoming representations and a final normalization and vocabulary head outside the block.
sections.code:
import math
import torch
from torch import nn

class TinyBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(width)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(width)
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(width, 3 * width)
        self.out = nn.Linear(width, width)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(width, 4 * width),
                                 nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * width, width))

    def forward(self, x):
        _, length, width = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(self.norm1(x)).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(width)
        future = torch.ones(length, length, device=x.device,
                            dtype=torch.bool).triu(diagonal=1)
        weights = scores.masked_fill(future, float('-inf')).softmax(dim=-1)
        x = x + self.out(weights @ v)
        return x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))

sections.title: Test behavior, not just output shape
paragraphs: First verify that output shape equals input shape and gradients reach every intended parameter. Next, change only future input positions and confirm earlier outputs are unchanged. Set both residual branches to zero and check that the block becomes an identity map. Finally, compare the explicit attention calculation with a trusted implementation on a tiny fixed input. This educational block omits padding masks and caching, so batches must contain fully valid sequences of equal length.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the Transformer equations for attention and FFNs together with the separate pre-LN reference. The original Transformer used post-LN, whereas TinyBlock deliberately normalizes before each residual branch. That distinction should be explicit when comparing its outputs or loading weights; this example is a small educational construction, not a compatible reproduction of an arbitrary pretrained architecture.

The SDPA reference offers a second implementation of the core attention operation for comparison. Set dropout to zero, match the causal mask and scale, and compare the explicit attention result before checking the complete block. The strongest small tests isolate separate properties: shape preservation, finite gradients, no effect from changed future inputs on earlier outputs, and identity behavior when both residual updates are zero. Passing them supports the implemented block's stated invariants. It does not validate omitted components such as padding handling, positional encoding, caching, tokenization, or a language-model training objective.

exercise.prompt: Why does matching input and output shapes fail to prove that a causal Transformer block is correct? Propose a stronger test.
exercise.answer: A wrong mask or an incorrect axis permutation can preserve every shape while allowing future leakage. In evaluation mode, alter tokens after position \(k\) and verify that outputs through \(k\) stay unchanged within numerical tolerance. Also inspect that forbidden attention weights are zero.

takeaways: Preserve the residual stream's shape and meaning.
Causality is a behavioral property that needs an explicit test.
